record.tranche_reason: The study changes the SAE architecture to separate token reconstruction from feature reconstruction and reports reconstruction and feature-composition results. This refines the possibility that some SAE reconstruction behavior depends on training design, but it does not directly test the dark-matter error analyses in V1–V5.
record.gate_note: The study reports reconstruction-error trends for common n-grams and comparisons of tokenized with non-tokenized SAEs; these bear on V6. It does not compare SAE errors with random equal-size errors, directly measure linear predictability of the error, or test whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts. Feature interpretability scores and other feature analyses are not rows because they do not directly measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper proposing Tokenized SAEs; it never cites or addresses the dark-matter analyses. Its reconstruction results (r6–r10) compare the authors' own architecture with baselines, which the rules exclude as tests. The frequency–MSE plots (r1–r5) measure how per-token error tracks token frequency in one SAE. They do not test linear predictability of the error (V1), cross-size predictability (V2), comparison with random errors (V3), the linear/nonlinear split (V4), loss of function in circuits or steering (V5), or whether dark matter mostly reflects training rather than representation (V6). The record's claim that it tests V6 overstates the link.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors argue that many RES-JB features reconstruct common unigrams and bigrams: an estimated 35–45% of features reconstruct common unigrams and about 70% common bigrams. They attribute this to training-token class imbalance combined with a lack of complex error signals. A per-token lookup bias gives better sparse-regime reconstruction (about 25% sparser at equal reconstruction) and 6–10x faster training. It also yields more complex features, but the feature-quality evidence rests on a 20-feature manual sample, and the Pythia results are preliminary and undertrained.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes Tokenized SAEs, adding a per-token lookup-table bias to the reconstruction path. It does not reproduce the dark-matter error analyses or their measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Reconstruction results vary with SAE architecture and layer; the paper reports a weaker frequency effect for bigrams than unigrams. Pythia results use undertrained SAEs.

fits_no_version.finding: In RES-JB SAEs on GPT-2 small, reconstruction MSE falls with unigram (and, more weakly, bigram) training-set frequency. The authors attribute this to training-data imbalance ('imbalanced regression').
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-token SAE reconstruction error is predicted by token/n-gram frequency in the training distribution, with rare tokens reconstructed worse.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a per-token lookup bias lowers NMSE and CE added at fixed L0. This holds on GPT-2 small layers 5–11 and on undertrained Pythia-1.4B SAEs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Part of SAE reconstruction error is token-identity information that a per-token bias path can absorb.

record.problems: Several reconstruction trends are reported only in figures without extractable numeric values. The Pythia SAEs use only 70M tokens and are described as undertrained. The paper does not include a random-error comparison or directly measure dark-matter error structure. The authors also caution that their manual feature-quality sample is limited.

untested.parts: No linear prediction of SAE error from input activations.
No per-token error-norm prediction across SAE sizes, no same-context failure analysis, and no scaling of error with size.
CE added is reported, but there is no comparison with random errors of equal norm.
No split of error into linear and nonlinear parts.
No circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term.

There is no decomposition of dark matter. The study does not test whether error mostly reflects training choices rather than representation structure. Architecture gains are reported only as the authors' own method's performance.

record.verdict_notes: The paper does not cite the dark-matter original. The reader's T5/V6 assignment and its supports/limits_scope labels rest on the study's own-method comparisons, which do not count as tests. A reconstruction improvement from an added token path says nothing about whether the residual error is a training artifact or representation structure.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure whether SAE error vectors are linear functions of input activations.
The study does not predict per-token error norms across SAE sizes, compare which contexts larger and smaller SAEs fail on, or test whether error vanishes with scale.
Although it reports added cross-entropy for SAE reconstructions, it does not compare the resulting loss with random errors of the same size.
The study does not split SAE error into linear and nonlinear components or test their proposed relationship to learned features and dictionary learning.
The study does not test whether analyses of circuits or steering lose behavior when the error term is omitted.

It tests a tokenized SAE architecture and reports frequency-linked reconstruction error and reconstruction comparisons, but does not separately test sparsity penalties, shrinkage, dead latents, end-to-end training, or whether dark matter mostly reflects training rather than representation structure.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tokenized SAE comparisons on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B
reader_labels.reason: Tokenized architectures improve reported reconstruction outcomes relative to non-tokenized counterparts, including lower CE added on all three reported Pythia layers (r6–r10).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The authors call these SAEs undertrained and describe the results as preliminary, so they do not establish how the baseline performs after full training (r8–r10).
